newsitem.title: LATVIA: Estonians lead drive to pan-Baltic finance market.
newsitem.headline: Estonians lead drive to pan-Baltic finance market.

text.p: Estonian banks and investment firms are leading the charge to forge a regional Baltic financial market spanning Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, analysts said on Thursday.
The latest cross-border move in the region populated by eight million people came as Estonian investment house Talinvest bought 87 percent of one of Lithuania's leading brokerages, Suprema.
"We are trying to market ourselves as one big region so that foreign investors take us more seriously," Talinvest sales and trading director Aare Tammemae told Reuters.
"The combined turnover of the three markets comes close to the turnover of other eastern European markets," he added.
Since breaking free from the former Soviet Union in 1991, the Baltic states have been committed market reformers with a pro-Western orientation.
Despite their small size, they have caught the attention of investors and are established on the emerging markets' circuit.
Estonian banks have spearheaded the move to make a pan-Baltic market a reality.
Leading bank Hansapank began the process last year when it bought a bank in Latvia. Fellow bank Tallinna Pank has just bought a 20 percent stake in Latvia's Saules Bank.
Both Hansapank and Tallinna Pank have said expansion to southernmost Baltic state, Lithuania, is on their agenda.

"This process will not necessarily speed up but an important part of the transition will be to create a more integrated financial market," Vlad Sobell, senior eastern Europe economist for Daiwa Securities told Reuters.
The Latvian and Estonian stock exchanges have also held talks to allow trade on each other's market without opening a local office.

Analysts said the pace is set by Estonians because their financial sector developed faster and because growth of the domestic market is limited by the country's size -- the smallest of the three countries.
Another reason is that althougfh all three states have suffered bank crises, Estonia's came out earliest, in 1992.
Analysts say the crisis caused a shake out and lessons were learnt that allowed a quicker development later.
Nomura Baltic specialist Claus Mansfeldt said that he expected more regionalisation, which was also due to the common economic and historical development of the three countries.
But he said that investors should also treat the three markets as separate.
"We do not treat them as one market other than that their destinies will be similar," Mansfeldt told Reuters.
